summary: Describes how to detect NAT devices between IPsec hosts and how to negotiate UDP encapsulation of IPsec packets through them in the Internet Key Exchange (IKE).

eli5.summary: A secure tunnel can get confused when a middle box rewrites addresses. This memo lets the two ends notice the rewriting and wrap their packets so the tunnel still works.

questions: how does ipsec work behind nat
why does ipsec use udp port 4500
subtitle: How two IPsec peers discover a NAT between them and agree to wrap their traffic in UDP so it survives the trip.

tldr.problem: IPsec traffic often breaks when a NAT sits between the two peers, because the NAT rewrites addresses and ports and cannot handle packets that are neither TCP nor UDP.
tldr.mechanism: During IKE Phase 1 the peers exchange vendor ID payloads to learn they both support NAT-Traversal, then exchange hashes of their IP addresses and ports (NAT-D payloads) to see whether anything was rewritten. If so, they move IKE to UDP port 4500 and negotiate UDP-encapsulated modes in Quick Mode.
tldr.outcome: Two peers can build IPsec tunnels through address translation. The companion RFC 3948 defines the UDP encapsulation itself. RFC 3947 is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3947 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be read with RFC 3948, which defines the UDP encapsulation it negotiates.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3947 describes how to detect one or more network address translation devices (NATs) between IPsec hosts, and how to negotiate UDP encapsulation of IPsec packets through them in the Internet Key Exchange (IKE).

The document has two parts. The first covers IKE Phase 1: finding out whether the other end supports NAT-Traversal and whether a NAT lies between the peers. The second covers Quick Mode: negotiating UDP-encapsulated IPsec packets and, when needed, sending the original source and destination addresses so that TCP/IP checksums can be fixed up after the NAT has changed the addresses.

The details of the UDP encapsulation are in RFC 3948. In the basic scenario the initiator is behind a NAT that translates addresses and ports, and the responder has a fixed static IP address. The protocol also works if both ends are behind a NAT, but how to locate the other end is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Some secret-message systems stop working when a middle box rewrites the addresses. This memo is the plan for noticing that and working around it.

sections.title: Detecting Support for NAT-Traversal
sections.content:
Support is discovered with vendor ID payloads. In the first two messages of Phase 1, a peer that supports this specification MUST send the vendor ID payload, and it MUST be received by both sides for the NAT-Traversal probe to continue.

The payload content is the MD5 hash of the text RFC 3947. The exact content in hex is 4a131c81070358455c5728f20e95452f.
sections.eli5: Each side first shows a secret handshake card. If both have the same card, they know the other one speaks this language.

sections.title: Detecting the Presence of NAT
sections.content:
To find a NAT, each peer checks whether the IP address or port changed along the path. Each end sends the other hashes of the IP addresses and ports of both peers, carried in NAT-D (NAT discovery) payloads, payload type 20. If both ends compute the same hashes, there is no NAT. If the hashes do not match, somebody translated an address or port, and NAT-Traversal is needed.

The hash is HASH(CKY-I | CKY-R | IP | Port), using the negotiated hash algorithm, with everything in network byte order. The IP is 4 octets for IPv4 and 16 octets for IPv6, and the port is 2 octets. The initiator and responder cookies are included to make precomputation attacks on the address and port impossible.

The first NAT-D payload holds the remote end's address and port, that is, the destination of the UDP packet. The remaining payloads hold possible local addresses and ports. A sender that does not know which of its addresses is used may send several local hashes, and NAT is detected if and only if none of them match. Normally there are only two NAT-D payloads.

The location of the NAT matters. If the first received NAT-D payload matches none of the local hashes, there is dynamic NAT between the peers and this end is behind it, so this end should start sending keepalives as defined in RFC 3948. The NAT-D payloads travel in the third and fourth packets of Main Mode, and in the second and third packets of Aggressive Mode.
sections.eli5: Each side writes down the return address it thinks it has and the one it sees on the envelope, scrambles both so nobody can read them, and compares. If the scrambles differ, someone changed the address on the way.

sections.title: Moving IKE to Port 4500
sections.content:
A NAT may change the IKE UDP source port, so recipients MUST be able to process IKE packets whose source port is not 500, and MUST reply to the source address and port of the packet they received.

Some IPsec-aware NATs misbehave, for example by never changing source port 500, or by using IKE cookies to sort traffic. The RFC's answer is to move IKE off port 500 as soon as possible. In Main Mode, once a NAT is detected, the initiator MUST change ports when it sends the ID payload, setting both UDP source and destination ports to 4500. All later packets to that peer MUST use port 4500, and the IKE data MUST be prefixed with a non-ESP marker, defined in RFC 3948, so that IKE and ESP traffic can be told apart.

The responder updates its state after it successfully processes that packet and answers all later IKE packets using the new port pair, for example UDP(4500,Y), where Y is the port the NAT assigned. Any implementation that supports NAT-Traversal MUST support negotiations that begin on port 4500. After the change, a Main Mode or Aggressive Mode packet with the old cookies arriving on port 500 SHOULD be discarded. A new exchange is processed normally, since the peer may have rebooted. If NAT-Traversal is enabled, the port in the ID payload MUST be set to 0.
sections.eli5: After spotting the mailroom, the two friends switch to a different mailbox number that the mailroom does not fiddle with, and use it for everything from then on.

sections.title: Quick Mode: Encapsulation and Original Addresses
sections.content:
After Phase 1 both ends know whether a NAT is present, but the final decision to use NAT-Traversal is made in Quick Mode, inside the SA payloads. Two new encapsulation modes are added: UDP-Encapsulated-Tunnel (3) and UDP-Encapsulated-Transport (4). If there is a NAT, UDP encapsulation SHOULD be used because normal modes may not work. If there is none, it SHOULD NOT be used, to avoid wasting bandwidth. An initiator SHOULD NOT propose both normal and UDP-encapsulated modes.

In transport mode, TCP and UDP checksums depend on the IP addresses, which the NAT changes. So both ends MUST send the original addresses with NAT-OA payloads (type 21), initiator address first and responder address second, in the first and second Quick Mode packets. The receiver can then update the checksums incrementally. In tunnel mode, both ends SHOULD NOT send original addresses. The ID type in a NAT-OA payload may only be an IPv4 or IPv6 address type.
sections.eli5: If the mailroom is in the way, the friends use the plain envelope. If they also need to tell each other their real home addresses, they put that in a short note inside.

sections.title: Initial Contact and Expiring NAT Mappings
sections.content:
For an INITIAL-CONTACT notification from a host behind a NAT, the source IP and port are not meaningful, because the NAT can change them. They MUST NOT be used to decide which IKE or IPsec SAs to remove. The receiver SHOULD instead remove all SAs associated with the same ID payload.

A NAT may drop mappings that are still in use, for example if the keepalive interval is too long or the NAT reboots. To recover, an end that is NOT behind a NAT SHOULD use the last valid UDP-encapsulated IKE or IPsec packet from the other end to learn the address and port to use. The host behind a dynamic NAT MUST NOT do this, since it would open a denial-of-service possibility. Keepalives cannot be used for this because they are not authenticated; an authenticated IKE packet or ESP packet can.
sections.eli5: If the mailroom forgets which door a friend uses, the friend outside the mailroom looks at the last real note that arrived to learn where to write back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists several effects. Advertising NAT-Traversal support to anyone watching introduces no new vulnerability. Address-based authentication loses its value once NATs are involved, so pre-shared keys in Main Mode would need group-shared keys for everyone behind the NAT. That is a large risk, since any group member could impersonate a VPN gateway, and group-shared keys are NOT RECOMMENDED.

The address hashes can be brute-forced: the private address space is small, ports are normally 500, and cookies are visible in the packet. That limits the work to 2^32 hash calculations, fewer with an educated guess of the private range. NAT-D and vendor ID payloads are not authenticated in Main Mode or Aggressive Mode, so an attacker can remove, modify or add them, causing denial of service or forcing UDP encapsulation and wasting bandwidth.

Sending original addresses in Quick Mode reveals the internal address to a peer that has already been authenticated. Updating addresses and ports on every valid authenticated packet can be abused by an attacker who reorders and re-injects packets, but the situation is fixed as soon as the attacker stops. Implementations SHOULD audit every mapping change.
sections.eli5: The address-scrambling can be guessed by a patient snoop, and the handshake cards are not locked, so a bad actor could tamper with them. The memo lists these risks and how to limit them.
